plain_language_meaning: A person or entity that leases or rents property from someone else (a tenant or renter).
legal_context: Used in lease agreements and property law to designate the tenant holding rights under a lease.
example_usage: The lessee agrees to pay the monthly rental amount on or before the fifth day of each calendar month.
source: Section 105, Transfer of Property Act, 1882 / Legal Glossary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: In spite of, regardless of, or despite what was previously stated.
legal_context: Used as a non-obstante clause in statutes and contracts to indicate that the clause overrides other conflicting rules.
example_usage: Notwithstanding anything contained in clause 4, the company may terminate this agreement with immediate effect.
source: Principles of Statutory Interpretation / Legal Glossary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: In this document, statement, or contract.
legal_context: A formal referencing adverb pointing to terms, covenants, or conditions contained within the same written instrument.
example_usage: The terms and conditions herein shall be binding upon both parties.
source: Legislative Drafting Manual, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: Mentioned or referred to previously in the text.
legal_context: Used to reference an entity, event, or asset established earlier in the document to prevent ambiguity.
example_usage: The aforementioned property shall be handed over in sound condition.
source: Legislative Drafting Manual, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: Legally responsible or obligated under the law to do something, pay damages, or face penalties.
legal_context: Used in civil and criminal jurisprudence to express accountability for debts, torts, or statutory offenses.
example_usage: The borrower remains liable for all unpaid amounts until full settlement.
source: General Clauses Act, 1897 / Legal Glossary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: A guilty mind or criminal intention to commit a wrongful act.
legal_context: A foundational doctrine in criminal law requiring proof that the accused had a wrongful mental state when committing the prohibited act.
example_usage: In the absence of proved mens rea or fraudulent intent, a mere breach of agreement cannot be converted into cheating.
source: Supreme Court of India criminal jurisprudence / Legal Glossary, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: The physical act or unlawful conduct that constitutes the external element of a crime.
legal_context: The tangible, voluntary conduct, deed, or omission forbidden by criminal law, which must coincide with mens rea.
example_usage: The prosecution established the actus reus by showing that the accused physically removed the files without authorization.
source: Supreme Court of India criminal jurisprudence / Legal Glossary, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: At first sight; based on first impression; accepted as correct until proved otherwise.
legal_context: Used to describe evidence that is sufficient to establish a fact or raise a presumption unless rebutted by contrary evidence.
example_usage: The court found prima facie evidence of fraud and directed registration of the complaint.
source: Legal Glossary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: A serious class of offense where a police officer has the legal authority to arrest the suspect without a warrant and begin investigation without prior court permission.
legal_context: Defined in criminal procedure codes to distinguish serious crimes (e.g. theft, stalking, cheating by personation) from non-cognizable offenses.
example_usage: Stalking under Section 78 BNS is a cognizable offense, allowing the investigating officer to register an FIR immediately.
source: Section 2(1)(g), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 / Section 2(c), Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

plain_language_meaning: An offense where a police officer cannot arrest without a warrant and cannot initiate an investigation without an order from a Magistrate.
legal_context: Applies to relatively less severe offenses (e.g. simple hurt, simple defamation) where judicial oversight is required before police action.
example_usage: Since the complaint disclosed only a non-cognizable grievance, the police recorded an NCR and referred the complainant to the Magistrate.
source: Section 2(1)(p), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 / Section 2(l), Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

plain_language_meaning: An offense for which the accused has a legal right to be released on bail upon providing appropriate surety or bond.
legal_context: Classified under the procedural schedule where bail is mandatory upon arrest if the accused is prepared to give bail.
example_usage: The offense was classified as bailable, so the police granted bail upon execution of a personal bond.
source: Section 2(1)(b), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 / Section 2(a), Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

plain_language_meaning: An offense where release on bail is not a matter of absolute right, but at the sound judicial discretion of the court.
legal_context: Applies to grave offenses where the court balances individual liberty against the interests of society and risk of flight or witness tampering.
example_usage: Extortion under Section 308 BNS is non-bailable, requiring the accused to move a formal bail application before the Sessions Court.
source: Section 2(1)(b), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 / Section 2(a), Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

plain_language_meaning: Made or done without surrendering, waiving, or prejudicing any existing legal rights or claims.
legal_context: Used in settlement communications and negotiations to prevent offers or statements from being used as admissions of liability in future proceedings.
example_usage: The settlement offer was sent on a without-prejudice basis and cannot be relied upon as an admission in court.
source: Section 17, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 / Section 23, Indian Evidence Act, 1872

plain_language_meaning: Among other things.
legal_context: A Latin phrase used in pleadings, judgments, and legal notices to highlight specific items from a broader list.
example_usage: The complaint alleges, inter alia, unauthorized access into the server and copying of proprietary database tables.
source: Legal Glossary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: With the necessary changes in points of detail having been made.
legal_context: Used when applying an existing statutory rule or contractual provision to a different situation with only relevant alterations.
example_usage: The arbitration procedure prescribed in Schedule A shall apply mutatis mutandis to all subsidiary agreements.
source: Legal Glossary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: Beyond legal power or authority; in excess of the legal powers conferred.
legal_context: Used in constitutional, corporate, and administrative law to declare an act, rule, or resolution void because it exceeds statutory jurisdiction.
example_usage: The High Court struck down the municipal regulation as ultra vires the enabling parent Act.
source: Constitutional and Administrative Law jurisprudence / Legal Glossary, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: In good faith; genuine; honest and without fraud or deceit.
legal_context: Used to describe intentions or actions performed honestly, without intent to cheat or commit deception.
example_usage: The purchaser established that they were a bona fide buyer for value without notice of the prior encumbrance.
source: Section 3(22), General Clauses Act, 1897 / Legal Glossary, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: In bad faith; dishonest, fraudulent, or motivated by an improper purpose.
legal_context: Used to challenge official actions or contractual breaches conducted with malicious intention or collateral motive.
example_usage: The petitioner argued that the transfer order was punitive and issued with mala fide intent.
source: Supreme Court of India jurisprudence / Legal Glossary, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: An obligation by one party to protect another against loss, damage, or legal liability, or to pay compensation for incurred losses.
legal_context: A contract or statutory obligation where the promisor saves the promisee from loss caused by the promisor's or any third party's conduct.
example_usage: The contractor provided a full indemnity covering any third-party claims arising from intellectual property infringement.
source: Section 124, Indian Contract Act, 1872 / Legal Glossary, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: From the very beginning.
legal_context: Refers to things that are legally invalid, void, or ineffective from the moment of inception, rather than becoming void later.
example_usage: An agreement with a minor is void ab initio under Indian contract law.
source: Legal Glossary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: In reality or in practice, even if not officially or legally established.
legal_context: Distinguishes actual existing practices or control from de jure (formally lawful) conditions.
example_usage: Although the director had resigned on paper, she continued as the de facto decision-maker of the firm.
source: Legal Glossary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: A legal rule preventing a person from denying or contradicting the truth of a representation they previously made.
legal_context: A statutory rule of evidence where an individual whose intentional declaration induced another to believe a thing cannot dispute it.
example_usage: By actively encouraging the vendor to deliver goods, the company was bound by estoppel from denying the order.
source: Section 121, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 / Section 115, Indian Evidence Act, 1872

plain_language_meaning: On its own motion; action initiated by a court or authority independently without an application from a party.
legal_context: Describes the exercise of inherent or supervisory jurisdiction where a court takes cognizance of a matter on its own initiative.
example_usage: The High Court took suo motu cognizance of the widespread environmental contamination reported in the news.
source: Supreme Court Rules, 2013 / High Court Constitutional Jurisprudence

plain_language_meaning: Under judicial consideration; currently being heard or pending determination by a court.
legal_context: Used to denote matters actively under adjudication where public commentary that could prejudice the trial may constitute contempt.
example_usage: The spokesperson declined to discuss the ongoing trial because the matter remains sub judice.
source: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 / Legal Glossary, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: Let the buyer beware; the buyer is responsible for inspecting the goods before purchase.
legal_context: A commercial rule of sales law establishing that the purchaser bears the risk regarding quality unless express warranties or fraud exist.
example_usage: Under the principle of caveat emptor, the buyer must satisfy themselves of the vehicle's roadworthiness before execution of sale.
source: Section 16, Sale of Goods Act, 1930 / Legal Glossary, Ministry of Law and Justice

plain_language_meaning: A matter that has already been conclusively decided by a competent court and cannot be relitigated between the same parties.
legal_context: A fundamental procedural rule barring any court from trying a suit on an issue that was directly in issue in a previously decided suit.
example_usage: The fresh claim was dismissed under Section 11 CPC on grounds of res judicata.
source: Section 11, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

plain_language_meaning: A formal written statement of facts sworn or affirmed to be true under oath administered by an authorized officer.
legal_context: Used as sworn written testimony in civil and criminal proceedings, subject to penalties for perjury if deliberately false.
example_usage: The petitioner submitted an affidavit affirming that no prior application had been filed before another forum.
source: Order XIX, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 / Section 3, Notaries Act, 1952

plain_language_meaning: Unforeseeable, extraordinary circumstances (such as acts of God or war) that prevent someone from fulfilling a contract.
legal_context: A contractual clause excusing performance upon occurrence of events beyond either party's control (provisional research entry).
example_usage: The supplier invoked the force majeure clause following the unprecedented port closure.
source: Provisional commercial law glossary (pending statutory codification review)

plain_language_meaning: A doctrine preventing a party from going back on a clear promise if the other party reasonably relied on it to their detriment.
legal_context: An equitable doctrine applied against private parties and government bodies to enforce promises made without formal consideration (provisional entry).
example_usage: The company relied on the doctrine of promissory estoppel to claim promised tax exemptions.
source: Provisional judicial doctrine glossary (pending statutory verification)
